$comment: What the generated sources are built from, and the decisions a machine cannot make.
Everything here is a choice: which release to read, which enums are part of this
package's public API, and what they are called. The generator makes none of them - it
only applies them - so a change in behaviour is a change in this file, reviewable on
its own.
Two sources, because Mojang changed how it publishes. `schemas` is the release this
package targets - the JSON schemas attached to a GitHub release, one file per type,
which is all Mojang publishes since 1.26.40 - and it is read through `import-schemas.js`
into `snapshot/enums.json`. `source` is the last `enums.html` Mojang published, at
1.26.40, kept for the enums the schemas do not describe: a schema exists only for a
type some packet field is declared with, and `LevelEvent`, `ActorDataIDs` and their
kind travel as plain integers. An enum in both is taken from the schemas.
Everything is pinned to a hash because Mojang deletes what it published: the branches
that carried `enums.html` were gone within a month of this project pinning one. The
pin is what makes a build reproducible after that happens, and the cached copy beside
it is the only one there will be.
The release this package targets: `metadata.zip` from the GitHub release of that
version, hashed. Its schemas list each enum's members without values - `GameType`
is `Undefined, Survival, ...` and nothing says `Undefined` is -1 - so the values are
read from `values`, the first later release whose schemas carry them as
`x-enum-binary-value`. The two agree on every member they share; every member of the
release that the values release lacks fails the import rather than being guessed.
1.26.50 and 1.26.51 are the same protocol, 2193; the hotfix is read because it is
what a client of this version runs. The values come from the 1.26.60 preview, 2211,
which is where `x-enum-binary-value` first appeared.
`schemaNames` maps an upstream enum name to the schema file that describes it where
the two differ: the documentation flattens `A::B` to `A__B` for most, and to something
else for a few.
The last `enums.html` Mojang published, from the 1.26.40 build: every enum in the
game, with values, which the JSON schemas above do not have and do not cover. Read
for the enums `snapshot/enums.json` lists as absent, and nothing else.
Pinned to the commit, not the branch, and the branch is gone now: `automated/1.26.40`
was deleted along with the rest of the `automated/*` family when the repository moved
to publishing releases. The cached copy in `snapshot/` is the only one there is.

thresholds.$comment: A parser that quietly returns a subset is worse than one that stops. If the document changes shape these fail the run instead of producing a small, plausible diff.

enums.$comment: Ours on the left, Mojang's on the right. An entry here is a decision that this enum is part of the package's public API; absence is not an oversight, it is a no. The upstream name is not stable across releases - LevelSoundEvent sits under Puv::Legacy at 748 and SharedTypes::Legacy later - which is why the mapping is data and not a convention.

$comment: Hand-written enums with no counterpart found in the docs, kept here so that the gap
is recorded rather than rediscovered. Each is either named differently upstream - to
be looked for among the 196 - or is not a protocol enum at all.
Not listed, and never generated: BehaviorPack, ResourcePack, StackPack, Experiment
and BlockProperty are payload structures, not enums. No source will ever supply them.

rules.$comment: Exceptions, so that adopting a generated enum never means renaming a call site. `aliases` keep the name this codebase has always used on the value vanilla documents; `extras` add what the document does not carry; `skip` drops what is not protocol - the dump lists preprocessor directives as if they were members.

BuildPlatform.$comment: 1.26.50 dropped the retired platforms - UWP, GearVR, tvOS and Windows Phone - and renamed Nx to Nintendo. A server validates a login against this list now, so the retired values are not kept as extras: a client reporting one is refused.

$comment: Names kept as this codebase has them, with one exception: 16 is
CraftRepairAndDisenchant upstream, which is the anvil as well as the grindstone. It
was called CRAFTING_GRINDSTONE here, and the upstream name is the accurate one.
The two deprecated container actions, 7 and 8, are gone from the release: the wire
never carried them, and their absence is why the selector an action is sent under
runs two behind the type from the lab table on. The last two lost their
`_DEPRECATEDASKTYLAING` suffix upstream at 1.26.50; the names here keep saying
deprecated, because they are.

ActorEvent.$comment: The hand-written copy had five members of the fifty-eight, and called 4 ARM_SWING where upstream calls it StartAttacking.

ContainerUiId.$comment: Every member is a `...Container`, which reads as noise on an enum already called that. Only the ones this server names are shortened; the other fifty-seven keep the documented name.

WindowIds.$comment: `CONTAINER_ID_` on every member of an enum called ContainerID. FIRST and LAST bound the range a server may open a window under, which is why they are worth having by name.

$comment: `FurnaceRecipe` and `FurnaceAuxRecipe` are gone from the document at 2168: the
Cereal conversion of CraftingDataPacket serialises recipes as one vector per shape,
so the tagged union these two discriminated no longer exists.
They are kept as extras because our CraftingDataPacket still writes the 748 format
and needs the two numbers to do it. They come out when that packet is converted -
which is the real fix, and is not this change.

ItemStackResponseResult.$comment: Sixty-eight ways for a request to go wrong, against the two this server distinguishes. Worth generating whole: a refusal currently says only `Error`, and every one of these is a reason we could be giving instead.

ItemDescriptorType.$comment: The kind of item descriptor a client's request carries: empty, a name, a MoLang expression or a tag. Up to 1.26.40 this package generated `ItemDescriptor::InternalType` under this name instead, an enum of the game's internals with two more members, which the schemas do not describe and nothing here used.

DisconnectReason.$comment: The hand-written copy stopped at 108 of these; the documented enum has a hundred and fifty, the last two of which - MissingStructureData and UnsupportedTransport - arrived at 2193 and are the two a client of this version is most likely to leave with. The aliases keep the names this codebase used for the members upstream prefixes with INTERNAL_ or TESTONLY_, and the two it calls deprecated.

$comment: Where the block state catalogue comes from and goes.
Captured from a Bedrock Dedicated Server, in two halves, because neither half alone
is the answer. The network palette is not on the wire - with hashed runtime ids
StartGamePacket carries only custom blocks - and the Script API answers a different
question: it reports the game's internal blocks, where a flattened name still carries
its legacy states, 56957 of them against the 17487 the network has.
So: which properties a block has comes from a *saved world*, whose sub chunk palettes
store exactly what the network carries; which values each takes comes from the game,
asked block by block rather than by property name - `age` is declared 0..15 game wide
and cocoa takes 0..2.
Validated against the third party dump this replaced: of 1218 blocks present in both,
1186 have identical property sets and the other 32 differ by one real rename
(`direction` became `minecraft:cardinal_direction`). Every shared property's values
agree exactly. `README-palette.md` is how to capture it again.
This is the last thing that came from pmmp/BedrockData other than item tags and the
creative list, and it was the one that needed a native mod hooking the server binary.
Mojang's own recipe files, from an unpacked Bedrock Dedicated Server of the version pinned
above. Not a third party's processed dump: these agree with the item table the same server
sends, which the dump they replaced did not - it disagreed with its own companion item map
for 58% of the names it used, and the recipe for a plank was dropped for it.
`bedrockServer` is a local path and the one thing here not in the repository: BDS is 58 MB
and Mojang's to distribute. Download the version above, unpack it, and point this at it,
or pass the path in `BEDROCK_SERVER` without editing this file. The output is committed,
so this is only needed to regenerate.
`itemAliases` brings the legacy names those files still use up to the ones the item table
knows - `reeds` for sugar cane, `sign` for an oak sign. Without it 52 recipes name something
no item table can resolve and are dropped.
$source: The behaviour pack directory, not one pack's recipes: BDS ships a 1.13 baseline in
`vanilla` and a layer per release on top, and the game composes them. The generator
reads `vanilla` and every `vanilla_<version>` up to the version pinned above, later
layers winning. `chemistry` and `experimental_` are not layers and are excluded.
$itemAliasOverrides: What the alias map above does not cover. Kept here rather than patched into the output,
so regenerating cannot quietly lose it - and listed one by one, so a name that stops being
needed is visible instead of hiding inside a rule.

$chain: Renamed when copper chains arrived and the iron one stopped being the only one.
The alias map beside this predates the rename, and 25 recipes in the older pack
layers still say `chain` - the game resolves them through its own table, which is
the thing this override stands in for.
